title: The Oasis Kingdoms: Taymāʾ, Dadān and Lihyān
subtitle: 1,200–300 BC · Taymāʾ, Nabonidus in Arabia, and the Kingdoms of Dadān and Lihyān

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: A chain of walled oasis kingdoms held the western Arabian corridor — Taymāʾ where a king of Babylon lived for a decade, the kingdom of Dadān and then Lihyān at al-ʿUlā, and Dūmah at the northern gate

entries.label: Taymāʾ, the walled oasis
entries.hint: A fortified oasis town of the northern Hejaz, its kilometres of mudbrick and stone wall enclosing wells and gardens, sitting where the caravan roads from Yemen, the Gulf and Mesopotamia met — one of the oldest continuously settled places in Arabia.
entries.note: the Saudi–German Tayma Project (from 2004); Arnulf Hausleiter, 'Tayma – an oasis in NW Arabia'; the Bronze Age wall covered in hejaz-prehistory-8000bc-1200bc.

entries.label: Taymāʾ and the Assyrians
entries.loc: Taymāʾ · recorded in the Assyrian annals
entries.hint: Tiglath-Pileser III took tribute from 'the people of Taymāʾ' in the 730s BC, and the oasis appears alongside Sabaʾ in the Assyrian records as a partner in the aromatics trade — a wealthy town the empire taxed from a distance.
entries.note: the annals of Tiglath-Pileser III; Israel Ephʿal, 'The Ancient Arabs' (1982).

entries.label: Nabonidus at Taymāʾ
entries.hint: The last king of Babylon left his capital, with his son Belshazzar as regent, and lived for a decade at Taymāʾ, which he rebuilt as a royal residence. His cuneiform inscriptions, a rock relief and Babylonian tablets have been found in the oasis.
entries.note: the Harran inscriptions of Nabonidus; the Nabonidus Chronicle; Hausleiter and Schaudig on the Taymāʾ cuneiform finds; the al-Ḥāʾiṭ (Padakku) rock relief.

entries.label: Nabonidus's oasis campaign
entries.loc: Dadān, Ḥibrā and Yathrib, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: On his way to Taymāʾ, Nabonidus took Dadān, Padakku, Ḥibrā (Khaybar), Yadīʿ and Yathrib — the deepest that any Mesopotamian army ever pushed into the western Arabian oasis chain, and the whole of it under Babylonian control for a decade.
entries.note: the Harran inscription H2 lists the oases taken; Hanspeter Schaudig's edition of the Nabonidus texts.

entries.label: The kingdom of Dadān
entries.hint: The oasis of Dadān was the seat of a kingdom of the 'Dadanites', named in the Hebrew Bible among the trading peoples, with its own kings, its sanctuary of the god Dhū Ghābat, and its own script and language.
entries.note: the Dadanitic inscriptions of Jabal Ikmah; Isaiah 21:13, Ezekiel 27:20; the French–Saudi excavations at Dadān.

entries.label: The kingdom of Lihyān
entries.hint: From about the 5th century BC the Lihyanites, a confederation whose rulers took the title 'king of Lihyān', succeeded the Dadanites at al-ʿUlā and built the most powerful oasis state of the northern Hejaz, which reached its height in the following centuries.
entries.note: Saba Farès-Drappeau, 'Dédan et Liḥyān: histoire des Arabes aux confins des pouvoirs perse et hellénistique' (2005).

entries.label: Dūmat al-Jandal, the northern gate
entries.hint: The great oasis of al-Jawf — 'the fortress of the Arabs' — was the cult centre for the northern tribes and the hinge of the routes to Syria and Mesopotamia; it was sacked by Sennacherib and later held by the Qedarites and then the Nabataeans.
entries.note: the Assyrian references to Adummatu; the Italian–Saudi excavations at Dūmat al-Jandal (Charloux).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Assyrian sack of Dūmah, Nabonidus's Arabian war, the turnover from Dadān to Lihyān at al-ʿUlā, and the oasis walls raised against the raiders

entries.label: Sennacherib and Esarhaddon at Dūmah
entries.hint: Sennacherib sacked Adummatu around 688 BC and carried off its gods; Esarhaddon later returned them with a client queen. The northern gate of the oasis chain was a repeated Assyrian target.
entries.note: Sennacherib's and Esarhaddon's inscriptions; Ephʿal (1982).

entries.label: The Babylonian conquest of the oases
entries.loc: from Dadān to Yathrib, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: Nabonidus's campaign of 552 BC took the oases one after another, and a Babylonian garrison and administration then held the northern Hejaz for the decade the king spent at Taymāʾ.
entries.note: the Harran inscriptions; the Verse Account of Nabonidus (hostile Babylonian propaganda).

entries.label: Dadān gives way to Lihyān
entries.hint: The change from the Dadanite kingdom to the Lihyanite one at al-ʿUlā — a new ruling group, a new royal title, a reworking of the sanctuary — was not necessarily peaceful, and the transition is one of the open problems of the region's history.
entries.note: Farès-Drappeau (2005); the epigraphic evidence for the dynastic change.

entries.label: The oases and the raiders
entries.loc: Taymāʾ, Dadān and Khaybar, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The walled towns of the northwest built and rebuilt their fortifications against the bedouin of the surrounding steppe — a constant low-level pressure the inscriptions record only obliquely, through the walls themselves and the occasional mention of an attack.
entries.note: the Taymāʾ and Dadān circuit walls; the general picture in Hoyland, 'Arabia and the Arabs' (2001).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The king-and-council government of the oasis states, Nabonidus's cult reform at Taymāʾ, the tolls on the caravans, and the self-governing Minaean colony at Dadān

entries.label: The oasis-kingdom constitution
entries.hint: The Dadanite and Lihyanite states were run by a king together with a council and by officials tied to the sanctuary. The many dedicatory and administrative inscriptions of Jabal Ikmah show a literate, organised polity, not a tribal chieftaincy.
entries.note: Farès-Drappeau (2005); the Dadanitic administrative texts.

entries.label: Nabonidus's cult reform and the Ṣalm of Taymāʾ
entries.hint: The Taymāʾ Stele records the introduction of the god Ṣalm of Hagam to the oasis, the endowment of his temple with land and revenue and a priest — a formal act of religious statecraft, at a moment when Nabonidus was also promoting his own devotion to the moon god Sîn.
entries.note: the Taymāʾ Stele (Aramaic, c.5th century BC, Louvre AO 1505); the debate over its relation to Nabonidus.

entries.label: The tolls on the incense road
entries.loc: Taymāʾ, Dadān and Dūmah, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The oasis states taxed the caravans that had to stop at their wells. Taymāʾ, Dadān and Dūmah each controlled a stretch of the western route and levied on what passed — the basis of their wealth and their reason to exist.
entries.note: Nigel Groom, 'Frankincense and Myrrh' (1981); the route reconstruction along the Darb al-Bakra.

entries.label: The Minaean colony at Dadān
entries.hint: The merchants of Maʿīn kept a resident, self-governing community at Dadān under an agreement with the local kings — foreign traders with their own law and cult at the northern hub of the incense road, their inscriptions found beside the Dadanitic ones.
entries.note: the Minaean inscriptions of al-ʿUlā; Farès-Drappeau (2005); Kitchen, 'Documentation for Ancient Arabia'.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Dhū Ghābat of Dadān, Ṣalm of Taymāʾ and the moon god Nabonidus brought, the standing stone alongside the colossal statue, and the beginnings of a Jewish presence in the north

entries.label: Dhū Ghābat and the gods of Dadān and Lihyān
entries.hint: 'He of the thicket', the chief god of al-ʿUlā, was worshipped at the sanctuary in the wadi alongside the other deities named in the hundreds of Jabal Ikmah inscriptions — a local pantheon with its own priesthood and its own festivals.
entries.note: the Dadanitic and Lihyanite dedicatory inscriptions; Farès-Drappeau (2005).

entries.label: Ṣalm of Taymāʾ and the moon god
entries.hint: The cult of Ṣalm at Taymāʾ — both aniconic and iconic — the Babylonian gods Nabonidus brought, above all Sîn the moon, and a layered religion at an oasis that sat where the Arabian, Aramaean and Mesopotamian worlds met.
entries.note: the Taymāʾ Stele; the Saudi–German excavation of the Taymāʾ sanctuary; Schaudig on Nabonidus and Sîn.

entries.label: The standing stone and the statue
entries.hint: The aniconic standing-stone tradition of the northwest sat alongside the large-scale figurative sculpture the Lihyanites also made — the same oasis culture worshipping in both idioms, betyl and colossus at once.
entries.note: the betyls of Taymāʾ and Dadān; the Lihyanite statues; the wider Arabian betyl literature.

entries.label: The first Jews of the northern oases
entries.loc: Taymāʾ, Khaybar and Wādī al-Qurā, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: Jewish communities are attested at Taymāʾ, Khaybar and along Wādī al-Qurā by the later centuries of this period and after — part of the same movement that produced the Jews of Yathrib, and a presence that lasted in the north into the 7th century AD.
entries.note: the firm evidence is from the Nabataean and Roman periods; Michael Lecker and Gordon Newby on the Jews of the northern Hejaz. Flagged: the earliest anchors here are thin.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The colossal statues of Lihyān, the inscribed canyon of Jabal Ikmah, the Taymāʾ Stele, the lion tombs of Dadān, and a family of alphabets

entries.label: The colossal statues of Lihyān
entries.hint: Over-life-size standing male figures in sandstone, some more than two metres tall, from the sanctuary at Dadān — the largest free-standing sculpture from ancient Arabia, in a distinct frontal Lihyanite style with traces of paint.
entries.note: the Lihyanite statues in the National Museum, Riyadh, and the al-ʿUlā site museum; Farès-Drappeau (2005).

entries.label: Jabal Ikmah, the open-air library
entries.hint: A canyon wall near al-ʿUlā covered with hundreds of Dadanitic and Lihyanite inscriptions — dedications, prayers, records of pilgrimage and offering — a UNESCO-listed archive of the ancient oasis written in stone over six centuries.
entries.note: the Jabal Ikmah inscriptions, added to the UNESCO Memory of the World register (2023); the Dadanitic corpus projects.

entries.label: The Taymāʾ Stele
entries.loc: Taymāʾ · now in the Louvre, Paris
entries.hint: The Aramaic stele of the god Ṣalm, with its relief of a priest before an altar under the winged disc, is one of the most important documents of 5th-century-BC Arabia and a centrepiece of the ancient Near Eastern collection of the Louvre.
entries.note: the Taymāʾ Stele (Louvre AO 1505), acquired by Charles Huber and Julius Euting in 1884.

entries.label: The lion tombs and the rock-cutting of Dadān
entries.hint: Rock-cut tombs in the cliffs of al-ʿUlā, some guarded by carved lions above the entrance — a Lihyanite funerary rock architecture that prefigures, and helped shape, the Nabataean tomb façades of Hegra a few kilometres away.
entries.note: the 'lion tombs' of Dadān; Farès-Drappeau (2005); Laïla Nehmé on the Dadān–Hegra architectural continuity.

entries.label: The Ancient North Arabian scripts of the northwest
entries.hint: Taymanitic at Taymāʾ, Dadanitic and Lihyanite at al-ʿUlā, and the Thamudic families across the region — a family of alphabets, cousins of the South Arabian and the Phoenician, in which the oasis peoples wrote their own distinct languages.
entries.note: M. C. A. Macdonald, 'Ancient North Arabian', in Woodard (ed.) (2008); the OCIANA database.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The reconstruction of the Nabonidus decade from scattered cuneiform, the decipherment of the al-ʿUlā scripts, and the recent turn from graffiti-reading to excavation

entries.label: Recovering the Nabonidus episode
entries.hint: The Harran inscriptions, the Nabonidus Chronicle, the hostile Verse Account, and the cuneiform tablets and rock relief found at Taymāʾ and along the route — from which the ten years of a Babylonian king in Arabia have been pieced together.
entries.note: Hanspeter Schaudig, 'Die Inschriften Nabonids von Babylon und Kyros' des Großen' (2001); Paul-Alain Beaulieu, 'The Reign of Nabonidus' (1989).

entries.label: Reading Dadanitic and Lihyanite
entries.hint: The decipherment of the al-ʿUlā scripts began with Euting and then Jaussen and Savignac's early-20th-century survey; the modern corpus projects and the Saudi–European surveys have since raised the number of legible inscriptions into the thousands.
entries.note: Antonin Jaussen and Raphaël Savignac, 'Mission archéologique en Arabie' (1909–22); the Dadanitic inscriptions database (OCIANA).

entries.label: From graffiti to excavation
entries.hint: The Saudi–German excavations at Taymāʾ from 2004, the French and Saudi work at Dadān, and the Royal Commission for AlUla's surveys have turned a region known mostly from rock inscriptions into an excavated stratified history.
entries.note: the Tayma Project reports (DAI); the RCU archaeological programme; the Dadān excavation publications.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The western incense road that every one of these towns lived on, the oasis farms that fed them, Dadān as the northern entrepôt, and the trade motive behind Nabonidus's decade

entries.label: The western incense road
entries.hint: The branch of the aromatics route running from Yemen through Najrān, Dadān, Taymāʾ and Dūmah toward Gaza and Mesopotamia was the reason every one of these oases existed as a town rather than a well.
entries.note: Groom, 'Frankincense and Myrrh' (1981); the caravan geography along the Darb al-Bakra.

entries.label: Oasis agriculture
entries.loc: Taymāʾ, Dadān and Khaybar, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The date palms, grain and vegetables of Taymāʾ, Dadān and Khaybar, irrigated from deep hand-dug wells, fed the towns and provisioned the caravans — a settled farming base without which the trade towns could not have functioned.
entries.note: the Tayma Project archaeobotany; the al-ʿUlā oasis surveys.

entries.label: Dadān, the northern entrepôt
entries.hint: Dadān was the hub where the incense road met the Lihyanite kingdom, where the Minaean colony traded, and where goods were transhipped for the Levant — the busiest and richest place in the northern Hejaz before the Nabataeans.
entries.note: Farès-Drappeau (2005); the mixed Minaean, Dadanitic and Lihyanite epigraphy of the site.

entries.label: Nabonidus's economic motive
entries.hint: The Babylonian king's decade at Taymāʾ is now often read as a bid to control the western Arabian trade routes and their wealth directly, at a time when the eastern routes and Babylon itself were troubled — commerce as much as piety or eccentricity.
entries.note: Beaulieu, 'The Reign of Nabonidus' (1989); the trade-route interpretation in the recent Taymāʾ literature.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The circuit walls and deep wells that made a large permanent town possible, and the monumental stone-cutting the Nabataeans would inherit

entries.label: The oasis walls and wells
entries.hint: The massive circuit walls of Taymāʾ — kilometres of them, in mudbrick on stone footings — the deep hand-dug wells, and the mud-lined channels that spread the water: the engineering that made a large permanent town possible on the desert edge.
entries.note: the Tayma Project's wall and hydrology studies; Hausleiter on the oasis water system.

entries.label: Monumental stone-cutting
entries.hint: The quarrying and carving of the Lihyanite statues and the rock tombs, and the dressed-stone architecture of the sanctuaries — a masonry tradition that the Nabataeans took over and scaled up into the great tomb façades of Hegra.
entries.note: Nehmé on the Dadān–Hegra continuity; the Lihyanite quarries at al-ʿUlA.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The one time Babylon governed a piece of western Arabia, the oases in the Hebrew record, the Minaean link to the south, and the Nabataean succession

entries.label: Babylon reaches the Hejaz
entries.hint: Nabonidus's residence at Taymāʾ was the one time a Mesopotamian empire directly governed a piece of western Arabia — an episode with no real parallel until the Ottomans two thousand years later.
entries.note: Beaulieu (1989); Schaudig (2001).

entries.label: The oases in the Hebrew record
entries.loc: Dadān and Taymāʾ · in the Hebrew Bible
entries.hint: Dadān and Taymāʾ are named in Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Job among the caravan peoples, and the oasis chain was in regular contact with the kingdoms of the southern Levant — a connection visible in the Aramaic script and the shared trade.
entries.note: Isaiah 21:13–14; Jeremiah 25:23; Ezekiel 27:20–21; Job 6:19.

entries.label: The Minaeans and the south
entries.hint: The resident Minaean traders at Dadān tied the northern Hejaz to the incense kingdoms of Yemen, and the Dadanitic and Minaean inscriptions of al-ʿUlA are found side by side — one oasis, two trading peoples, one road.
entries.note: the Minaean epigraphy of al-ʿUlA; Farès-Drappeau (2005).

entries.label: The Nabataean succession
entries.hint: As Lihyān declined the Nabataeans moved into the region, making Hegra their southern city and taking over the trade Dadān had run — the folio's link forward to the Nabataean kingdom, which has its own folio.
entries.note: a forward reference; nabataean-312bc-106ce covers Hegra and the Nabataean south.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: A thousand years of walled, literate, trading oasis kingdoms in the western corridor, and the dated Babylonian decade that anchors their chronology

entries.label: The oasis-town civilisation of the northwest
entries.loc: Taymāʾ, Dadān, Khaybar and Dūmah, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: For a thousand years a chain of walled, literate, irrigated, trading towns held the western Arabian corridor, each with its own king, its own gods and its own script — a civilisation invisible in the standard histories, recovered from its own inscriptions.
entries.note: Farès-Drappeau (2005); Hoyland, 'Arabia and the Arabs' (2001); the al-ʿUlA and Taymāʾ archaeological programmes.

entries.label: The Nabonidus decade as an anchor
entries.hint: The ten years of a dated Babylonian king in Arabia give the whole northwestern oasis chronology a fixed point that the region's own undated rock inscriptions otherwise entirely lack.
entries.note: Beaulieu (1989); the use of the Nabonidus synchronism in dating the Taymāʾ and Dadān sequences.

entries.label: The thread continues — Lihyān, the Nabataeans and Hegra
entries.hint: The folio ends at 300 BC with Lihyān rising to its height. The following centuries bring the peak of the Lihyanite kingdom and then the Nabataeans, whose city at Hegra and whose kingdom at Petra are covered in the folio that follows.
entries.note: a forward reference: nw-arabia-106-632 (from the Roman annexation to the coming of Islam) is planned but not yet built; nabataean-312bc-106ce is already built.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Women named in the oasis inscriptions, the workers of the caravan road, and a Babylonian court living a decade in exile in an Arabian oasis

entries.label: Women in the oasis inscriptions
entries.hint: Women appear at Dadān and Taymāʾ as dedicators, as priestesses and as property-holders, named in their own right in the Dadanitic texts — a visibility comparable to that in the contemporary South Arabian record and greater than in most of the ancient Near East.
entries.note: the Dadanitic inscriptions naming women; comparison with the South Arabian material in the epigraphic literature.

entries.label: The workers of the caravan road
entries.loc: the western incense route, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The drovers, guides, well-keepers and porters who moved the caravans between the oases, and the enslaved people the inscriptions list among temple and household property — the labour under the trade the kings taxed.
entries.note: the incidental references in the Dadanitic and Minaean epigraphy; the general picture in Hoyland (2001).

entries.label: Nabonidus's court in exile
entries.hint: The Babylonian officials, soldiers and servants who spent a decade with their king at Taymāʾ, far from home — a displaced imperial community in an Arabian oasis, visible in the administrative cuneiform tablets excavated there.
entries.note: the Babylonian tablets from Taymāʾ; the Verse Account's complaint about the king's absence from Babylon.
